newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German opposition want Kohl to sack Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German opposition want Kohl to sack Waigel.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrat (SPD) and Green parties joined forces on Monday to turn the screws on beleaguered Finance Minister Theo Waigel by tabling a parliamentary motion calling for his dismissal.

The parties also want parliament to to adopt as its own a sharply-worded statement made by the Bundesbank last week criticising Waigel's plan to revalue the central bank's assets to help Germany qualify for Europe's single currency.

"Waigel is unbearable as finance minister," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told a news conference to launch the resolutions, which the opposition parties want parliament to vote on later this week.
"He has used his relatively long term of office to make all the possible mistakes a finance minister could make," he said.

Waigel is due to state the government's position on the controversial revaluation plan in a special debate in parliament on Wednesday and the opposition parties could use that as an opportunity to debate their motions.
They want parliament to call on Chancellor Helmut Kohl to dismiss Waigel in a resolution which would not be binding but would embarrass the already beleaguered government if passed.
Finance Ministry spokeswoman Barbara Eckrich said Waigel was not at all worried about the motion, which she believed was the first parliamentary bid to oust Waigel.
"We are calm and relaxed about this," she told a regular government news conference.
Waigel, who last week became Bonn's longest-serving finance minister after eight years in the job, said then he had the confidence of the coalition and the chancellor and saw no reason to resign.

Scharping slammed Waigel and Kohl for what he called an unprecedented combination of record debt and unemployment and said their plan to revalue the Bundesbank's assets had prompted a serious loss of trust in the economic and financial world.
"It (the revaluation plan) has thrown up serious questions about Germany's reliability," he said.
Waigel has stubbornly stuck by his plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold an currency assets and rejected the central bank's claims that it is an assault on its fabled independence.

On Monday Waigel said he would try to reach agreement with the bank before proposing the legal changes that would allow Bonn to benefit from the revaluation, but said he would proceed with the plan even without the Bundesbank's assent.

Waigel, struggling to fill a huge budget gap because of tax shortfalls and higher-than-forecast spending resulting from high unemployment, hopes the revaluation plan would reap 20 billion marks ($11.7 billion) and partly ease the government's debt burden and help Germany to meet the single currency entry criteria.

But some members of Kohl's coalition have echoed the Bundesbank's opposition to the plan, raising the possibility that the veteran chancellor might not be able to muster a majority to push the controversial measure through parliament.

One senior CDU official told Reuters there were numerous deputies in the Free Democrats (FDP) junior coalition partners who loath Waigel and would relish the chance to embarass him in parliament. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
